title: Sea-urchin shell outlines match liquid drops flattened by gravity

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Sea-urchin shell outlines match liquid drops flattened by gravity

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The vertical outlines of regular sea-urchin shells are the forms of liquid drops depressed by gravity (with the pull of the tube-feet), their degree of flattening varying with the tension or strength of the shell: strong shells (Palaeechinus) stay nearly spherical, soft flexible ones (Phormosoma) are most flattened.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: but we have no difficulty in seeing that the various forms represented in a series of sea-urchin shells are no other than those which we may easily and perfectly imitate in drops.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XV, “On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures”; topic “Form of sea-urchins”. Scope: tests of regular echinoids

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch15-09: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.66

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Shape is directly measurable and the drop model gives quantitative predictions. Public scans support a taxonomically restricted shape test, but paired mechanical variables are sparse, so the full causal claim is only partly resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit axisymmetric capillary-drop models to 3D echinoid tests and test whether flattening covaries with shell stiffness and tube-foot loading. Systematic residuals or absent stiffness-shape covariation would refute the stated account.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Preserved tests omit living soft-tissue loading.

Shell stiffness and tube-foot force are rarely paired with scans.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Drop profiles and a flattening index are standard geometric measurements, so the main series can be compared with an explicit physical family of shapes. Public images and scans cover only part of the regular echinoids, and plate-level mechanical properties are mostly in separate papers. A quantitative fit can still reject a pure drop model for the conical and collapsed forms, while agreement on the ordinary flattened series would remain compatible with several rounded geometries.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure test height, diameter and plate thickness on vertical outlines of regular echinoids, fit each profile to a sessile-drop solution over a range of Bond numbers, and treat plate thickness as a proxy for shell tension. The claim would be supported if flattening increases as plate rigidity falls and the residuals match drop profiles; it would be weakened if spherical and flattened tests share the same plate thickness or if the outlines fit ellipses or cones as well as drops.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Aristotle's lantern and apical buoyancy, which Thompson himself invoked for some outlines, are extra forces a single drop parameter does not absorb.

Open scans and profile photographs are sparse for flexible forms such as Phormosoma and for Palaeechinus.
